scenario.name: PikeRed Research & MITRE T1574.012 — Abusing the .NET CLR Profiler: VHDX MotW Bypass & Trusted-Binary Loader Chain (KeePass.exe -> clr.dll)
scenario.overview: Think of a classic neighborhood post office with brass P.O. boxes lining the back wall, a parcel scale counter, a blue street mailbox outside, and angled mail sorting chutes. At the neighborhood post office counter, a sender slips tiny coded lines onto the back of ordinary postcards and drops them one by one into the mail sorting slot. In this real-world scenario, the intruder bypasses the normal inspection rule to reach the brass p.o. box sorting wall, then approaches the postal scale & stamp window disguised as a regular visitor. The postmaster reviews the evening dispatch ledger and spots hundreds of oddly coded postcards all mailed to the exact same remote P.O. box. In this scenario (T1553.005, PikeRed Research & MITRE T1574.012, Abusing the .NET CLR Profiler: VHDX MotW Bypass & Trusted-Binary Loader Chain (KeePass.exe -> clr.dll)), the attacker follows one continuous intrusion path so each later Step can show the exact handoff that makes the next stage possible. The attack unfolds in one continuous arc: vHDX Container Mounting and attrib +h +s, then process Environment Seeding, then clr.dll ProfilingAPIUtility LoadProfiler. Steps #1–#3 walk that chain end-to-end by covering VHDX Container Mounting and attrib +h +s, then Process Environment Seeding, then clr.dll ProfilingAPIUtility LoadProfiler, while the Process Hierarchy tab keeps the Parent → Child spawn tree visible so you can see which trusted process launched the next payload. Primary detection correlates Sysmon Event 1 with the documented host and network chain.

stages.subtitle: Initial Access & Defense Evasion (T1553.005 - Mark-of-the-Web Bypass / T1564.001 - Hidden Files)
stages.description: At the neighborhood post office counter, a sender slips tiny coded lines onto the back of ordinary postcards and drops them one by one into the mail sorting slot. Specifically in Step 1, the intruder bypasses the normal inspection rule to reach the brass p.o. box sorting wall while everyday visitors and the postal clerk go about their routine. The user mounts Payroll_2026.vhdx (a weaponized virtual hard disk). Windows assigns drive E: through vhdmp.sys (logging VHDMP Operational Event ID 12) and does not copy NTFS Zone.Identifier Mark-of-the-Web streams onto files inside the mounted volume, so SmartScreen never sees the inner binaries. The attacker marks KeePass.exe and ProfilerLoader.dll under E:\.runtime\ with hidden and system attributes (attrib +h +s), leaving only a decoy shortcut visible in Explorer. Mounting a VHDX keeps the MotW alternate data stream on the outer .vhdx file only; every executable staged inside the volume therefore launches without the download warning that would normally block unknown files. Pairing +h +s attributes further hides the real host binary and profiler DLL from casual directory listings even when hidden files are shown. In the documented EventID 12 exchange from Initial Access Delivery (Weaponized .vhdx) to Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap, Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap responds with ACK 12 (confirming that the explorer.exe request succeeded on Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 Stage 2: Process Environment Seeding (COR_ENABLE_PROFILING=1, COR_PROFILER, COR_PROFILER_PATH)). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ explorer.exe / ⇠#1 ACK 12) from Node ① (#1 Initial Access Delivery (Weaponized .vhdx)) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Signed KeePass.exe -> clr.dll -> ICorProfilerCallback::Initialize).

stages.description: Because each postcard carries valid postage and a harmless street address, the postal clerk stamps them smoothly and sends them down the brass sorting chute. Here in Step 2 inside the post office, the intruder smuggles copied records out past the postal scale & stamp window in tiny disguised batches without disturbing the registered certified mail safe. When the user runs the decoy shortcut on E: the launcher sets COR_ENABLE_PROFILING=1, COR_PROFILER={B7A3F9E1-4C2D-4A8B-9E10-C1D2E3F4A5B6}, and COR_PROFILER_PATH=E:\.runtime\ProfilerLoader.dll on the child process environment block, then starts the legitimate signed KeePass.exe without touching HKCU registry profiler keys (registry-free loading on .NET 4+). CLR profiling variables in the process environment block are inherited only by the child KeePass.exe instance, avoiding persistent HKCU or HKLM Environment keys that blue teams often monitor. Sysmon Event ID 1 can still capture the full Environment field on process create. In the documented EventID 1 exchange from Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap to Mounted VHDX Volume (MotW Stripped + attrib +h +s), Mounted VHDX Volume (MotW Stripped + attrib +h +s) responds with ACK 1 (confirming that the E:\.runtime\KeePass.exe request succeeded on Mounted VHDX Volume (MotW Stripped + attrib +h +s) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 Stage 3: mscoree.dll -> clr.dll!ProfilingAPIUtility::LoadProfiler & ICorProfilerCallback::Initialize Execution). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ E:\.runtime\KeePass.exe / ⇠#2 ACK 1) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 Mounted VHDX Volume (MotW Stripped + attrib +h +s)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Signed KeePass.exe -> clr.dll -> ICorProfilerCallback::Initialize).

stages.title: Stage 3: `mscoree.dll` -> `clr.dll!ProfilingAPIUtility::LoadProfiler` & `ICorProfilerCallback::Initialize` Execution
stages.subtitle: Defense Evasion & Execution (T1574.012 - COR_PROFILER / Trusted-Binary Loader Chain)
stages.description: One harmless postcard at a time, an entire confidential binder is smuggled right out of the post office without ever raising the heavy parcel-inspection alarm. In this final step inside the post office, the intruder approaches the postal scale & stamp window disguised as a regular visitor until the postmaster dispatch ledger catches the mismatch. During KeePass.exe startup, mscoree.dll initializes clr.dll, which reads the profiling environment variables, loads ProfilerLoader.dll from E:\.runtime\ via LoadLibraryW, resolves the COM class factory, and calls ICorProfilerCallback::Initialize inside the trusted KeePass.exe process. No CreateRemoteThread or cross-process injection APIs are required because the signed host voluntarily loads the attacker DLL (The CLR startup path treats COR_PROFILER_PATH as a trusted diagnostics hook, so the malicious DLL gains code execution inside a process whose image is digitally signed and allowlisted Sysmon Event ID 7 logs the unsigned DLL load from the mounted volume, and NET Runtime Event ID 1022 records that a profiler initialized successfully). The CLR startup path treats COR_PROFILER_PATH as a trusted diagnostics hook, so the malicious DLL gains code execution inside a process whose image is digitally signed and allowlisted. Sysmon Event ID 7 logs the unsigned DLL load from the mounted volume, and .NET Runtime Event ID 1022 records that a profiler initialized successfully. In the documented EventID 7 exchange from Mounted VHDX Volume (MotW Stripped + attrib +h +s) to Launcher Setting COR_ENABLE_PROFILING=1 & COR_PROFILER_PATH, Launcher Setting COR_ENABLE_PROFILING=1 & COR_PROFILER_PATH responds with ACK 7 (confirming that the KeePass.exe request succeeded on Launcher Setting COR_ENABLE_PROFILING=1 & COR_PROFILER_PATH and completing the final execution objective of PikeRed Research & MITRE T1574.012, Abusing the .NET CLR Profiler: VHDX MotW Bypass & Trusted-Binary Loader Chain (KeePass.exe -> clr.dll)). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ KeePass.exe / ⇠#3 ACK 7) from Node ③ (#3 Mounted VHDX Volume (MotW Stripped + attrib +h +s)) to Node ④ (#4 Launcher Setting COR_ENABLE_PROFILING=1 & COR_PROFILER_PATH), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Signed KeePass.exe -> clr.dll -> ICorProfilerCallback::Initialize).

steps.simpleExplanation: During KeePass.exe startup, mscoree.dll initializes clr.dll, which reads the profiling environment variables, loads ProfilerLoader.dll from E:\.runtime\ via LoadLibraryW, resolves the COM class factory, and calls ICorProfilerCallback::Initialize inside the trusted KeePass.exe process. No CreateRemoteThread or cross-process injection APIs are required because the signed host voluntarily loads the attacker DLL (The CLR startup path treats COR_PROFILER_PATH as a trusted diagnostics hook, so the malicious DLL gains code execution inside a process whose image is digitally signed and allowlisted Sysmon Event ID 7 logs the unsigned DLL load from the mounted volume, and NET Runtime Event ID 1022 records that a profiler initialized successfully).
steps.howItWorksInPractice: The CLR startup path treats COR_PROFILER_PATH as a trusted diagnostics hook, so the malicious DLL gains code execution inside a process whose image is digitally signed and allowlisted. Sysmon Event ID 7 logs the unsigned DLL load from the mounted volume, and .NET Runtime Event ID 1022 records that a profiler initialized successfully.
steps.diagramAlignment: On the diagram, Step #3 completes inside Node ⑤ (KeePass.exe with ProfilerLoader.dll) with clr.dll load order captured on Node ⑥ (Sysmon EID 7 and .NET Runtime 1022).
steps.detectionAndEvidence: Documented in Sysmon Event ID 7 and .NET Runtime Event ID 1022: correlate a signed .NET binary loading an unsigned DLL from a VHDX-mounted path with a successful profiler initialization message.
